International Affairs Week was scheduled for March 6 to 10, 1950 [Source 1]. Organized by YMCA International Affairs committee co-chairmen Joan Bruckheimer and Jim Hipkins, the week was designed to promote student interest in global issues under slogans such as "International Understanding Or Chaos" and "Think, Discuss, Act, Make International Understanding A Reality" [Source 1].

![G. Bromley Oxnam](https://pub-6b4b0bceb63e48c1af6578ad09beb2e5.r2.dev/1950-03-01/images/0001_Page%201_img2.webp)

The week opened on Monday with a speech in chapel by Bishop G. Bromley Oxnam, vice-president of the World Council of Churches and Bishop of the New York area [Source 1]. It officially closed on Friday with a panel discussion featuring various foreign students from the Ohio Wesleyan campus [Source 1].

The eight students who advanced were Phoebe Babbage of East Aurora, N. Y.; Bruce Gensemer of Cleveland Heights, O.; George Iden of Bloomingburg, O.; Peter Latimer of Cleveland Heights, O.; Jerry Sell of Delaware; Jack Van Horn of Pulaski, Pa.; Robert E. answer.text:
In January 1980, the Stuyvesant Hall Governing Board unanimously voted to implement a new security policy requiring that only Stuyvesant Hall residents be admitted to the building after 11:30 p.m. [Source 1]. All non-residents entering after 11:30 p.m. were required to be escorted by a Stuyvesant Hall resident [Source 1]. 

Under this policy, student security aides remained on duty until 7:00 a.m. to check student identification cards against a resident list or verify residency using dorm-coded keys [Source 1]. Unescorted visitors were required to call the resident they were visiting, who had to come to the lobby and escort them to the room [Source 1]. Stuyvesant Hall Resident Life Counselor Lewis Herndon noted that the policy was designed to curtail violence, vandalism, and unauthorized visitors, and it successfully increased individual billings for damages rather than campus-wide hall billings [Source 1, Source 2].

At the 1982 All-Ohio meet at Ohio State, the Ohio Wesleyan women's track team set three new school records in relay events [Source 1]. 

The 880-yard relay team, consisting of Pebbles Muller, Amanda Osborn, Lynn Rhoden, and Sabrina Spencer, placed sixth with a time of 1:50.2, breaking the 1979 record of 1:51.2 by one second [Source 1]. The distance medley relay team of Liz Einfeldt, Nena Lenfest, Barb Sweeney, and Margie Morris finished in fifth place with a record time of 13:17.1, breaking the previous mark of 13:18 [Source 1]. Additionally, the two-mile relay team of Einfeldt, Lenfest, Sweeney, and Lisa Foster set a new record with a time of 10:14, surpassing the prior record of 10:20 [Source 1].

answer.text:
## Addressing Outdated Communications Infrastructure in 1987

In 1987, Ohio Wesleyan University addressed its outdated telephone infrastructure, which had been in place since 1974 and caused widespread frustration due to insufficient lines and central switchboard bottlenecks [1987-03-25-25, 1987-10-14-3]. Physical Plant Director John Tombarge began exploring system options and negotiating with vendors for a modern replacement estimated at $1.2 million [1987-03-25-25]. In September 1987, the Board of Trustees formally approved $50,000 for a feasibility study to hire a professional telecommunications consultant [1987-09-30-0, 1987-10-14-3]. Vice President of Business Affairs Louis Szalontai noted that the consultant was tasked with researching new technology and evaluating the costs of leasing versus purchasing a system, aiming for completion by 1992 [1987-10-14-3].

## Consolidating Academic Support Services in 2000

In the fall of 2000, the university resolved fragmented academic support by creating the Academic Resource Center (ARC) on the third floor of the R.W. Corns Building [2000-09-13-3]. Directed by former high school math teacher Donna Dawson, the ARC consolidated three previously separate programs into a single location: the Writing Resource Center, the Academic Skills Office, and the Qualitative Skills Center [2000-09-13-3]. Prior to the consolidation, the Writing Resource Center and Academic Skills Office operated separately in University Hall, while the Qualitative Skills Center had been located in the Hamilton-Williams Campus Center and was inactive for several years [2000-09-13-3]. The centralized ARC provided students with unified access to writing tutors, math and economics assistance, study skills training, computers, reference materials, and dedicated study space [2000-09-13-3].

answer.text:
Austin Hall closed in 1984, and plans to renovate the residence hall into Austin Manor—a living unit for students and retired alumni—were formed in the fall of 1986 [Source 1]. Financing for its restoration was assembled in 1987, but work could not begin until tax credit approval based on Austin's historic status was obtained [Source 1]. 

While credit from the Interior Department declaring Austin an historic site in Ohio was enthusiastically approved, the Philadelphia office initially turned it down [Source 1]. Following an appeal, the tax credit was approved, allowing work to begin [Source 1]. University President David Warren estimated that the renovated building would be ready for an occupant by November or December of 1988 [Source 1].

answer.text:
## Early Childhood Center Hands-On Learning Support (1997)

In 1997, Ohio Wesleyan's Early Childhood Center (ECC) offered experiential, hands-on learning support designed for preschool children ages three to five, centered on multi-sensory exploration, child-directed projects, and peer cooperation [1997-01-22-17].
![an OWU student assists a child with a project at the Early Childhood Center](https://pub-6b4b0bceb63e48c1af6578ad09beb2e5.r2.dev/1997-01-22/images/0005_Page%205_img1.webp)
Under director Dr. Leslie Mass and head teacher Melinda Radabaugh, the center encouraged children to explore all of their senses through practical, interactive activities such as observing and feeding mice or worms in three aquariums, cutting apples for snack time, and constructing miniature houses using varied materials [1997-01-22-17]. Rather than being bound by a fixed elementary curriculum, the ECC established broad goals and turned the children's specific interests—such as leaves gathered on nature walks, insects, castles, and dragons—into long-term projects [1997-01-22-17]. Learning support was provided by professional teachers working alongside 29 OWU student assistants employed through work-study and Student Assistantship programs [1997-01-22-17]. Children participated in free-choice activities like painting, reading, puzzles, and basic computer work, while older children were encouraged to help younger peers who struggled, creating an empowering peer-tutoring dynamic alongside early writing, problem-solving, and decision-making development [1997-01-22-17].

## Academic Resource Center Centralized Support (2000)

In contrast, the Academic Resource Center (ARC) established in the fall of 2000 provided structured, centralized academic support tailored specifically to Ohio Wesleyan university students [2000-09-13-3]. Located on the third floor of the R. W. Corns Building and directed by former high school math teacher Donna Dawson, the ARC consolidated three previously separate campus resource entities into a single facility [2000-09-13-3]. 

The consolidated units included the Writing Resource Center directed by Ulle Lewes, which provided tutor assistance on papers, resumes, and standardized writing test preparation; the Academic Skills Office, staffed by trained interns offering guidance in test preparation, organizational skills, and stress management; and the Qualitative Skills Center, managed by Dawson to assist students with economics and math courses up to Calculus II [2000-09-13-3]. Rather than informal exploratory play, the ARC provided hands-on support through target-specific individual tutoring, dedicated study space, three computer terminals, and a reference library of writing materials [2000-09-13-3].

## Key Differences in Learning Support

The two centers reflected distinct pedagogical models appropriate to their respective age groups. The 1997 Early Childhood Center prioritized **sensory exploration, open-ended creativity, and flexible project-based discovery** for early childhood development, utilizing OWU undergraduates as mentors and role models [1997-01-22-17]. In contrast, the 2000 Academic Resource Center focused on **higher education academic remediation and skill mastery**, bringing writing, quantitative reasoning, and study-skills tutoring under one administrative umbrella to aid college students in specific academic subjects [2000-09-13-3].
